newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan mulls new atomic fuel but faces resistance.
newsitem.headline: Japan mulls new atomic fuel but faces resistance.

text.p: Despite growing public concern about the use of nuclear power, the Japanese government is exploring new ways of harnessing the atom to meet its huge appetite for energy.
A report issued by a government panel this week urged the nuclear industry to use plutonium mixed with uranium as a new fuel in commercial reactors.

But industry sources say the government will face a tough task to convince a sceptical public of the merits of the mixed oxide (MOX) fuel after a string of mishaps, including a major oil spill, stoked controversy over the nation's ambitious nuclear programme.

The worries were underscored this month when oil from a wrecked Russian tanker washed up along a strip of coast where Japan's biggest concentration of nuclear reactors is found, threatening to clog up their water-cooling systems.
Although the fears proved unfounded, the threat of a shutdown at the plants again focused public attention on Japan's heavy reliance on clusters of nuclear reactors.
Resource-poor Japan uses nuclear power for around 30 percent of its energy.

A Trade Ministry official briefing reporters about the panel's proposal said MOX would be crucial to ensuring Japan's energy demands are met, given a setback in its plans to introduce fast-breeder reactors.

Public doubts about Japan's nuclear power programme have intensified since a coolant accident at Japan's prototype fast-breeder reactor, Monju, in December 1995. However, there are few suggestions about how Japan might realistically solve its energy problems without resorting to nuclear energy.
Nuclear industry sources said public concern would hamper any effort to adopt the new plutonium-based fuel. Plutonium is currently not used as a fuel in Japanese nuclear plans.
"We don't believe we have reached a stage where we can ask the local inhabitants to accept it (the use of MOX fuel)," one electricity industry source said.

The governors of Niigata, Fukushima and Fukui prefectures, which have the most nuclear power plants, have told the central government they cannot accept MOX fuel until the cause of the Monju accident is made clear.

The Monju accident, caused by a massive leak of liquid sodium, has halted the plant's operations indefinitely. No one was injured in the accident but an official in charge of investigating a cover-up of the accident committed suicide.
Plutonium, which is extracted from spent nuclear fuel together with uranium, can be re-used either as MOX fuel or in fast-breeder reactors. MOX is used in several countries, including Germany.
The Monju accident has disrupted the government's plan to introduce a fast-breeder reactor, making MOX fuel the only other means of re-using plutonium.
Fast-breeder reactors burn plutonium refined from spent fuel of conventional reactors. In the process, they produce more fuel than they consume.
The government report said Japan should aim to have about three or four nuclear reactors using MOX fuel by 2000.

The use of MOX fuel is "becoming even more important" because of the delay to Japan's nuclear programme caused by the Monju accident, the report said. Japan was hoping to start using fast-breeder reactors sometime around 2030.
Japan had about 4.7 tonnes of plutonium at the end of 1993, of which some 3.4 tonnes are likely to be fissile, according to latest government figures available.
